note: Curated Nigerian maternal Q&A knowledge pack. Cached on-device; grounds the offline SmolLM and doubles as fine-tuning data (modal/finetune.py). Safe, plain-English, WHO/Nigeria-aligned. NOT a diagnosis.

items.q: What foods should I eat during pregnancy?
items.a: Eat a mix every day: beans, eggs, fish or meat, moimoi, green vegetables (like ugu, ewedu), fruits, and pap or yam. Take your iron and folic acid tablets from the clinic. Drink plenty clean water.

items.q: Which foods should I avoid in pregnancy?
items.a: Avoid alcohol and smoking completely. Avoid raw or undercooked meat/eggs, unpasteurised milk, and too much caffeine. Wash fruits and vegetables well before eating.

items.q: How much water should I drink?
items.a: Drink about 8 cups of clean water a day, more when it is hot. Dark urine means you need more water.

items.q: I am vomiting a lot in early pregnancy, what can I do?
items.a: Eat small meals often, try dry foods like biscuits or bread in the morning, sip water or ginger. If you cannot keep any food or water down, or you feel very weak, go to the clinic — you may need help so you don't get dehydrated.

items.q: What can I do about heartburn?
items.a: Eat smaller meals, avoid oily and peppery food, and don't lie down right after eating. Sleep with your head raised a little. Ask your clinic before taking any medicine.

items.q: My legs and feet are swelling, is it normal?
items.a: Mild swelling of the feet late in the day can be normal. Rest with your legs raised. BUT if your face or hands suddenly swell, or you get a bad headache or blurred vision, go to the clinic the same day — it can be a danger sign.

items.q: How do I deal with back pain in pregnancy?
items.a: Sit with your back supported, avoid lifting heavy things, wear flat shoes, and rest often. Gentle stretching helps. If the pain is severe or comes with bleeding or tightening, go to the clinic.

items.q: Is it safe to have sex during pregnancy?
items.a: In a normal pregnancy, sex is usually safe. Stop and see your clinic if you have bleeding, pain, or your water breaks, or if your health worker told you to avoid it.

items.q: How often should I go for antenatal care (ANC)?
items.a: Start antenatal care as early as possible. WHO recommends at least 8 visits. Your clinic will give you your dates — attend every one, even when you feel fine.

items.q: Why should I take folic acid and iron?
items.a: Folic acid helps your baby's brain and spine form well. Iron prevents anaemia (low blood), which is common and dangerous in pregnancy. Take them daily as your clinic gives you.

items.q: What is anaemia and why does it matter?
items.a: Anaemia means low blood. It makes you tired and weak and can be dangerous at delivery. Eat iron-rich food (beans, liver, green vegetables), take your iron tablets, and go to the clinic if you feel very weak or your palms/eyes look pale.

items.q: How do I know I am in labour?
items.a: Signs include regular tightening pains that get stronger and closer together, a show (mucus with a little blood), or your water breaking. Go to your place of delivery when pains are strong and regular, or if your water breaks.

items.q: My water broke but no pains, what do I do?
items.a: Go to your clinic or hospital now, even without pains. Note the time and colour of the water. If the water is green or smells, tell the health worker immediately.

items.q: When should I count the baby's movements?
items.a: From about 28 weeks, your baby should move regularly each day. If you notice the baby moving much less than usual, drink water, lie on your side and count. If movements are still reduced, go to the clinic the same day.

items.q: How can I prepare for a safe delivery?
items.a: Plan to deliver at a health facility with a skilled birth attendant. Pack a bag early (clothes for you and baby, your ANC card, pads, money for transport). Know how you will get there quickly, day or night.

items.q: Is malaria dangerous in pregnancy?
items.a: Yes. Malaria in pregnancy is dangerous for you and the baby. Sleep under a treated mosquito net every night, take the preventive tablets (IPTp) your clinic gives, and go to the clinic quickly if you have fever.

items.q: Can I take medicine when I am pregnant?
items.a: Do not buy and take drugs on your own. Some medicines harm the baby. Always ask your clinic or pharmacist first, even for pain or malaria.

items.q: How do I start breastfeeding?
items.a: Put the baby to your breast within the first hour after birth. Give only breast milk for the first 6 months — no water, no other food. Feed on demand, day and night. The first yellow milk (colostrum) is very good for the baby.

items.q: My breasts are painful and I have a fever after birth
items.a: This can be a breast infection (mastitis). Keep breastfeeding or expressing milk, rest, and go to the clinic — you may need treatment. Go quickly if you feel very unwell.

items.q: How do I care for the baby's cord?
items.a: Keep the cord clean and dry. Do not put anything on it unless your health worker says so. If the cord area becomes red, swollen, smells, or has pus, take the baby to the clinic now.

items.q: My newborn's skin and eyes look yellow
items.a: Yellow skin or eyes in a newborn (jaundice) needs checking. Take the baby to the clinic or hospital. If the baby is also not feeding well, is very sleepy, or floppy, go now.

items.q: When does my baby need vaccines?
items.a: At birth: BCG, OPV0, Hepatitis B. Then at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, and at 9 months (measles, yellow fever). They are free at the health centre — do not miss them, they protect against killer diseases.

items.q: How do I know if I have high blood pressure danger (pre-eclampsia)?
items.a: Warning signs are a bad headache, blurred vision or seeing spots, swelling of the face and hands, and pain in the upper belly. This is an emergency — go to the hospital now.

items.q: I feel very sad or cannot sleep after birth
items.a: Many mothers feel low after birth. Rest when you can, accept help, and talk to someone you trust. If the sadness is deep, lasts more than two weeks, or you have thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, tell a health worker — help is available.

items.q: How can I space my next pregnancy (family planning)?
items.a: Waiting at least 2 years before the next pregnancy is healthier for you and your baby. Your clinic offers free family planning methods — ask them which is best for you.

items.q: How much weight should I gain in pregnancy?
items.a: Some weight gain is healthy and expected as your baby grows. Eat balanced meals rather than eating for two. Your clinic will weigh you at each visit and tell you if anything needs attention.

items.q: I don't have appetite, I am not eating much
items.a: Eat small amounts more often instead of big meals, and choose foods you can manage like pap, fruit, beans or eggs. Keep taking your clinic tablets. If you are losing weight or feel very weak, tell your clinic.

items.q: I feel like eating chalk or clay (uwa), is it okay?
items.a: Craving chalk, clay or sand is not safe — it can carry germs and may be a sign of low blood (anaemia). Do not eat them. Tell your clinic so they can check your blood.

items.q: What are good snacks between meals?
items.a: Good snacks include fruit (banana, orange, pawpaw), groundnut, boiled egg, roasted plantain, or moimoi. They keep your strength up without too much sugar or oil.

items.q: I am constipated, what can I do?
items.a: Eat more fruit, vegetables and beans, and drink plenty of water. Move around gently each day. Do not take strong laxatives on your own — ask your clinic if it does not improve.

items.q: I get painful cramps in my legs at night
items.a: Leg cramps are common in pregnancy. Stretch the leg and gently rub it, and try to walk a little in the day. Tell your clinic if the pain is constant, or one leg is swollen, red and hot.

items.q: Is it normal to have more discharge from my private part?
items.a: A little more clear or whitish discharge without itching or bad smell is usually normal in pregnancy. Keep clean and wear cotton pants. If it itches, smells bad, or has blood, go to the clinic.

items.q: My private part is itching with smelly discharge
items.a: This may be an infection that needs treatment. Do not douche or use harsh soap inside. Go to your clinic so they can check and treat it safely.

items.q: I have mild headaches, what should I do?
items.a: Rest, drink water, and eat regularly, as tiredness and hunger can cause headaches. Do not buy strong painkillers yourself. If the headache is severe, will not go, or comes with blurred vision or swelling, go to the hospital now.

items.q: I feel dizzy and like I will faint
items.a: Stand up slowly, sit or lie on your side, and eat and drink something. Dizziness can come from low blood or not eating. If you actually faint, have chest pain, or bleed, go to the clinic quickly.

items.q: Why am I so tired all the time?
items.a: Tiredness is very common, especially early and late in pregnancy. Rest when you can, eat well and take your iron tablets. If you are extremely weak or your palms and eyes look pale, tell your clinic — it may be low blood.

items.q: I am passing urine very often, is something wrong?
items.a: Passing urine often is normal as the womb presses on your bladder. Keep drinking water. But if it burns, or you have fever or back pain when urinating, go to the clinic — it may be an infection.

items.q: I have piles (swelling around my back passage)
items.a: Piles are common in pregnancy. Avoid constipation by eating fruit and vegetables and drinking water, and don't strain in the toilet. Tell your clinic if there is a lot of bleeding or severe pain.

items.q: I have stretch marks and my belly skin itches
items.a: Stretch marks and mild belly itching as the skin stretches are normal. Keep the skin moisturised and drink water. If the itching is severe all over your body, tell your clinic.

items.q: My whole body itches badly, especially my hands and feet
items.a: Severe itching all over, especially on the palms and soles with no rash, should be checked at the clinic soon — it can be a sign of a liver problem in pregnancy that needs monitoring.

items.q: I can't sleep well at night
items.a: Try sleeping on your side with a pillow between your knees, avoid heavy food or too many drinks near bedtime, and rest in the day when you can. If worry is keeping you awake, talk to someone you trust.

items.q: I feel short of breath sometimes
items.a: Feeling a little breathless when active is common as the baby grows and presses up. Rest and slow down. But if you are suddenly very breathless, have chest pain, or your lips look blue, go to the hospital now.

items.q: I feel tightening in my belly that comes and goes
items.a: Practice tightenings (false labour) that come and go and then stop can be normal, especially later on. Rest and drink water. If the tightenings become regular, painful and closer together, or your water breaks, go to your place of delivery.

items.q: I am bleeding from my private part while pregnant
items.a: Any bleeding from the private part in pregnancy should be checked. Go to the clinic or hospital now, even if it is small. If it is heavy or with strong pain, treat it as an emergency.

items.q: I have severe pain in my belly
items.a: Severe or constant belly pain in pregnancy is not normal — go to the hospital now. Do not wait or take medicine on your own.

items.q: I have a fever, what should I do?
items.a: Fever in pregnancy can be malaria or another infection and should not be ignored. Go to the clinic to be tested and treated the same day. Do not take drugs on your own.

items.q: What if I have a fit or convulsion?
items.a: Fits or convulsions in pregnancy are a life-threatening emergency. Whoever is around should take you to the hospital immediately and keep you safe on your side while going.

items.q: I fell down, could it harm the baby?
items.a: After a fall or blow to the belly, go to the clinic to be checked, even if you feel fine. Go straight away if you have bleeding, belly pain, tightening, or the baby is moving less.

items.q: What happens at an antenatal (ANC) visit?
items.a: The health worker checks your blood pressure, weight, urine and blood, listens to the baby, gives you tablets and jabs, and answers your questions. Attend every visit and carry your ANC card.

items.q: Why do they check my blood pressure at the clinic?
items.a: High blood pressure in pregnancy can be dangerous for you and the baby, often with no symptoms early on. Checking it at each visit helps catch problems early so you can be treated in time.

items.q: Why do they take my blood at ANC?
items.a: Blood tests check for low blood (anaemia), your blood group, and infections like HIV and syphilis so they can be treated to protect you and the baby. It is a normal, important part of care.

items.q: Why do they test my urine?
items.a: The urine test checks for infection, sugar, and protein that can point to problems like high blood pressure or diabetes in pregnancy. It helps your clinic catch things early.

items.q: Do I need a scan (ultrasound) in pregnancy?
items.a: A scan checks the baby's growth, position, due date and the water around the baby, and is helpful at least once in pregnancy. Your clinic will tell you when to do it. It is safe for the baby.

items.q: Should I test for HIV in pregnancy?
items.a: Yes — the HIV test is a normal part of ANC. If you are positive, safe medicine can protect your baby from getting it (PMTCT). Knowing early keeps both of you healthy.

items.q: Why do they give me a tetanus injection?
items.a: The tetanus jab protects you and your newborn from tetanus, a deadly infection that can enter through the cord. It is safe and free — take all the doses your clinic gives.

items.q: Why must I carry my ANC card?
items.a: Your ANC card holds your test results, blood pressure, dates and treatment. Carry it to every visit and to delivery so any health worker can care for you correctly, even in an emergency.

items.q: What are the IPTp tablets they give at the clinic?
items.a: IPTp are tablets given during ANC to prevent malaria, which is dangerous in pregnancy. Take them as directed at your visits, in addition to sleeping under a treated net every night.

items.q: How should I use a mosquito net?
items.a: Sleep under a treated mosquito net every single night, tucked in under the mattress, from early pregnancy. It protects you and the baby from malaria at the time you are most at risk.

items.q: My iron tablets make my stool black and I feel constipated
items.a: Black stool from iron tablets is normal and not harmful. To ease constipation, drink water and eat fruit and vegetables. Keep taking the tablets — do not stop unless your clinic says so.

items.q: When should I start taking folic acid?
items.a: Folic acid is best started before pregnancy or as early as you can, because it protects the baby's brain and spine in the first weeks. Get it free at the clinic and take it daily.

items.q: Which foods help build my blood?
items.a: Iron-rich foods help build blood: beans, liver, meat, fish, eggs, and dark green vegetables like ugu and ewedu. Eating them with orange or other fruit helps your body absorb the iron. Keep taking your iron tablets too.

items.q: Can I take agbo or herbal mixtures in pregnancy?
items.a: Avoid agbo and herbal mixtures in pregnancy — the strength is not controlled and some can harm the baby or bring on early labour. If you feel unwell, go to the clinic instead.

items.q: My body hurts, what medicine can I take?
items.a: Do not buy painkillers yourself, as some are not safe in pregnancy. Rest and use warm support, and ask your clinic or pharmacist which pain relief is safe for you.

items.q: Do I need deworming in pregnancy?
items.a: Deworming may be given at the clinic after the first three months to help prevent anaemia. Do not take it on your own — let your health worker decide the right time and dose.

items.q: I feel stressed and worried all the time
items.a: Some worry is normal, but too much stress is not good for you. Rest, talk to someone you trust, and share your worries at the clinic. If you feel overwhelmed or hopeless, tell a health worker.

items.q: I am afraid of giving birth
items.a: Fear of delivery is very common. Learning what to expect and planning to deliver with a skilled attendant helps you feel ready. Share your fears with your health worker — they are there to support you.

items.q: My husband or family are not supporting me
items.a: Pregnancy is easier with support. Try to talk with someone you trust and let the clinic know your situation. If anyone is hurting you or threatening you, tell a health worker — you deserve help and safety.

items.q: Is it safe to exercise while pregnant?
items.a: Gentle activity like walking and light stretching is good in a normal pregnancy. Avoid heavy lifting, hard falls and getting too tired. Stop and see your clinic if you have pain, bleeding or tightening.

items.q: How much rest and sleep do I need?
items.a: Try to sleep about 7-8 hours at night and rest during the day when you can. Lie on your side, especially later in pregnancy. Balancing rest with gentle activity keeps you well.

items.q: Can I lift heavy loads or do hard work?
items.a: Avoid lifting very heavy loads and long hours of hard work, especially later on. Take breaks, drink water and ask for help. Rest and see your clinic if you feel pain, tightening or bleeding.

items.q: I had a little bleeding after sex, is it serious?
items.a: Light spotting after sex can happen, but any bleeding in pregnancy should be checked. Avoid sex until you are seen, and go to the clinic. If bleeding is heavy or with pain, treat it as an emergency.

items.q: When should I go to the hospital once labour starts?
items.a: Go when your pains are strong, regular and closer together, when your water breaks, or if you see fresh blood. If in doubt, it is safer to go early — do not deliver at home alone.

items.q: How can I cope with pain during labour?
items.a: Move around, change positions, breathe slowly, and have someone support you. Drink small sips and empty your bladder often. The skilled birth attendant will guide you and help with pain.

items.q: I am scared of having a caesarean (CS)
items.a: A caesarean is done to keep you and the baby safe when normal birth is risky, and it saves lives. Delivering at a health facility means the team can act quickly if it is needed. Ask your health worker any questions you have.

items.q: Can I just deliver at home?
items.a: It is much safer to deliver at a health facility with a skilled birth attendant, because emergencies like heavy bleeding can happen suddenly and need fast help. Plan ahead how you will get there.

items.q: What should I pack in my hospital bag?
items.a: Pack your ANC card, wrapper and clothes for you, clothes and a cap for the baby, sanitary pads, toiletries, and money for transport and care. Get it ready by the eighth month.

items.q: Should someone come with me to the delivery?
items.a: Yes, having someone you trust with you during labour is helpful and comforting. Arrange this early with the person and your place of delivery.

items.q: How do I plan for an emergency during delivery?
items.a: Decide now where you will deliver, how you will get there quickly day or night, and keep some money set aside for transport and care. Save a number for help and tell your family the plan.

items.q: I feel my breast milk is not enough for the baby
items.a: The more the baby suckles, the more milk you make, so feed often on demand and let the baby empty one breast before the other. Drink water and eat well. If the baby is not wetting nappies or losing weight, go to the clinic.

items.q: My nipples are cracked and sore from breastfeeding
items.a: Cracked nipples often come from the baby not latching deep enough onto the breast. Make sure the baby takes in the dark part, not just the tip, and rub a little breast milk on after feeds. Ask your clinic to check the latch if it does not improve.

items.q: How often should I breastfeed my baby?
items.a: Feed on demand, whenever the baby wants, day and night — usually 8 or more times a day. Do not wait for the baby to cry hard. For the first 6 months give only breast milk, no water.

items.q: I am HIV positive, can I breastfeed my baby?
items.a: Yes, if you take your HIV medicine as directed, you can breastfeed safely and it is recommended. Give only breast milk and keep all your clinic appointments so both of you stay protected.

items.q: How do I keep my newborn warm?
items.a: Dry the baby, dress and cap the head, and hold the baby skin-to-skin on your chest, especially small babies. Keep the room free of cold draughts. If the baby feels cold, floppy or won't feed, go to the clinic now.

items.q: What position should my baby sleep in?
items.a: Lay your baby on the back to sleep, on a firm flat surface, with nothing over the face. This lowers the risk of cot death. Keep the baby close to you but not under heavy covers.

items.q: How and when should I bath my newborn?
items.a: Wait a day or two before the first bath, and keep the baby warm during it. Use clean warm water, bath quickly, and dry well, keeping the cord dry. You do not need to bath many times a day.

items.q: What are the danger signs in a newborn?
items.a: Go to the clinic now if the baby is not feeding, is very sleepy or floppy, has fast or hard breathing, is very hot or cold, has fits, yellow skin, or a red, smelly cord. Newborn illness can move fast.

items.q: My baby is very sleepy and not feeding well
items.a: A newborn that will not wake to feed or is floppy needs to be seen quickly — take the baby to the clinic or hospital now. Keep the baby warm and keep trying to feed on the way.

items.q: My baby cries a lot, what can I do?
items.a: Check if the baby is hungry, wet, too hot or cold, or wants to be held, and offer the breast. Holding and gentle rocking helps. If the baby also has fever, vomiting, or will not feed, go to the clinic.

items.q: How much bleeding is normal after birth?
items.a: Some bleeding that slowly reduces over days to weeks is normal after birth. But if you soak a pad in an hour, pass big clots, feel faint, or the blood smells bad with fever, go to the hospital now.

items.q: Do I need a check-up after giving birth?
items.a: Yes. You and the baby should be checked after birth, including in the first week and around six weeks, to make sure you are healing well and to start family planning and vaccines. Go sooner if anything worries you.

items.q: How do I care for stitches after delivery?
items.a: Keep the area clean and dry, change pads often, and wash your hands before and after. It heals over a couple of weeks. Go to the clinic if it becomes very painful, swollen, smells, or leaks pus.

items.q: My baby missed a vaccine, what should I do?
items.a: Take the baby to the health centre as soon as you can — the vaccine can still be given (catch-up) so the baby stays protected. Carry the baby's immunization card.

items.q: Can breastfeeding stop me getting pregnant again?
items.a: Full breastfeeding can help delay pregnancy only in the first 6 months, if your period has not returned and you feed often day and night. It is not certain — ask your clinic about a reliable family planning method too.

items.q: How do I make my drinking water safe?
items.a: Use water from a safe source, and if you are unsure, boil it or treat it before drinking. Store it in a clean, covered container. Safe water protects you and the baby from infection.

items.q: How do I keep food and hands clean to avoid sickness?
items.a: Wash your hands with soap before cooking and eating and after the toilet. Cook food well, wash fruits and vegetables, and cover food from flies. This prevents infections that are harmful in pregnancy.

items.q: I am expecting twins, what should I know?
items.a: Twins are a joy but need closer care, as there is a higher chance of anaemia, high blood pressure and early labour. Attend all your ANC visits, eat and rest well, and plan to deliver in a hospital.

items.q: I am a teenager and pregnant, is it more risky?
items.a: Young mothers can have a healthy baby with good care, but there is a higher risk of problems, so early and regular ANC is very important. Eat well, take your tablets, and plan to deliver at a facility. The clinic is there to support you without judging.

items.q: I am over 35, does age affect my pregnancy?
items.a: Many women over 35 have healthy pregnancies, but there is a slightly higher chance of high blood pressure and other issues, so regular ANC matters. Attend all visits and share any concerns with your health worker.

items.q: Can I keep working while pregnant?
items.a: You can usually keep working in a normal pregnancy. Take breaks, sit and rest, drink water, avoid heavy lifting and long standing, and don't get too tired. Slow down and see your clinic if you feel unwell.

items.q: Is it safe to travel a long journey while pregnant?
items.a: Short and needed trips are usually fine, but for long journeys stand and stretch often, drink water, and carry your ANC card. Avoid travel near your due date, and do not travel if you have bleeding or other danger signs.

items.q: Should I hide my pregnancy from people?
items.a: You do not need to hide your pregnancy for it to be safe — that is only a belief. What truly protects you and the baby is attending antenatal care, eating well, and planning a facility delivery.

items.q: Can the shape of my belly tell if it is a boy or girl?
items.a: The shape of your belly does not tell the baby's sex — that is just a belief. Only a scan can suggest it. Focus your energy on eating well and attending your clinic visits.

items.q: Is it true I should eat for two people now?
items.a: You do not need to eat for two — that is a myth and can lead to unhealthy weight. Eat balanced meals with a little extra, plenty of vegetables and fruit, and take your clinic tablets.
